lawyer:
Shaiukat Ali Khan with Karmakshyam Nath Sen, Fazlul Haque Khan Farid, Advocates
 ----- For the Appellants.  
AQ Abdur Rashid, Advocate ----- For the State.
parties:
Dr. Golam Rahman and 2 others ----- Appellants  
Vs  
The State ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
The appellants have been convicted under section 16 of the Drugs (Control) Ordinance, 1982 passed by the Judge, Drugs Court in Drugs Case No. 23 of 1985 and appellant No. 1 has been sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3 years and to pay a fine of Tk. 10,000/- in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 6 months while appellant Nos. 2 and 3 were sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 2 years and to pay a fine of Tk. 5,000/-each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3 months each. 

 2. The prosecution case, in short, is, that the Superintendent of Drug, Mymensingh, inspected M/S Rahman Clinic, a medicine shop of Mymensingh Town, on 8.6.85 accompanied by a Magistrate, and police force and seized 49 items of banned and unregistered drugs from the shop in presence of witnesses and prepared the seizure list. Thereafter he lodged a First Information Report with the Kotwali Police Station against the appellant Nos. 2 and 3, on the accusations that they were salesmen and by keeping the unregistered and banned drugs in the shop eon-i-n-14W offence under section 16 of the Drug (Control) Ordinance, 1982 and upon such accusations Kotwali PS Case No. 7(6) of 1985 was started. The Superintendent after filing the First Information Report also submitted a report on 12.6.1985 in the Court of Drugs Judge, Dhaka as a complainant against the appellant No. 1 Dr. Golam Rahman and appellant Nos. 2 and 3 Samir Kumar Das alias Sumir Kumar Das and Bishnupada Bhattacharjee on the accusations, inter alia, that Dr. Golam Rahman practices sitting in M/s. Rahman Clinic and Appellant Nos. 2 and 3 were salesmen of the said clinic, and on inspection on 8.6.85 he found huge quantity of unregistered and banned medicines in that shop and seized 49 items of those medicines. And the appellants committed the offence punishable under section 16 of the said Oidinance by keeping in stock those medicines and by exhibiting the same for sate. Against Dr. Golam Rahman further allegation was that he signed some papers for renewal of drug licences and paid licence fee for the said shop. 

 4. The prosecution examined 3 witnesses in this case. 

 5. From the trend of cross-examination it appears that the defence of the accused appellants was that they have been falsely implicated in this case out of grudge at the instance of the Deputy Commissioner of Mymensingh over some incidents with him and that no medicine was seized from the Rahman Clinic. 

 6. Appellant No. 1, in course of examination under section 342 CrPC, pleaded not guilty of the charge and submitted a written statement stating that on transfer from the Barisal Medical College he joined the Mymensingh Medical College as an Assistant Professor of Pathology only two days before the date of occurrence and he was neither the owner of M/S Rahman Clinic nor was its manager. He was a member of Mymensingh Club of which the Deputy Commissioner of Mymensingh was the President. Over the administration of the club a dispute arose between him and the Deputy Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner had also some ill-feeling against him in connection with requisition of some of his land for the construction of Inter Districts Bus Terminal and also for refusal to sell medicine for the wife of the Deputy Commissioner on credit by the salesman. As a result of which the Deputy Commissioner in collusion with the complainant got an inspection held in (1) Rahman Clinic, (2) Sekander Drug Centre and Sonali Medical Hall. Although no unregistered medicine was found in the Rahman Clinic yet his Chamber attendant Bishnopada and salesman Samir Kumar were arrested along with two other persons from two other shops and a case was filed in the Kotwali Police Station under section 16B of the Drug Ordinance read with Special Powers Act in which he was not made an accused. But later on at the direction of the Deputy Commissioner the Superintendent of Drug filed this case in the court implicating him as accused No. 1. Appellant No. 1 stated that he signed some paper on behalf of Rahman Clinic in absence of his father, the proprietor of the shop, and merely he practises sitting in the said clinic. 

 7. PW 1, the Superintendent of Drugs, stated that drug licence of M/s. Rahman Clinic stands in the name of Golam Haider who was 90 years old. Doctor Golam Rahman, son of Golam Haider, practises sitting in the clinic. PW 1 proved an application for renewal of drug licence filed by Dr. Golam Rahman Exbt. No. 1 and a Chalan showing payment of drug licence fee in his name, Ext. 2 and an application signed by Dr. Golam Rahman for withdrawal of the order of suspension of the drug licence. PW 1 also stated that accused Samir Kumar Das and Krishnapada were salesmen of the shop and on inspection he found 49 items of banned and unregistered medicines and seized those under a seizure list prepared and signed by him, Ext. 4 and those medicines were banned under Schedules I, II, and III of the Drugs (Control) Ordinance. He proved his report filed in the court, Ext.5 and the signature of Bishnapada on the seizure list Ext. 4/2. He stated that at the time of inspection he took AZM Rafiqur Rahman, the Magistrate, Mymensingh with him. He proved the seized medicine, Material Ext. I which were with the police in connection with another criminal case and those were the drugs of the three medical shops viz, M/s. Rahman Clinic, Sonali Medical Hall and Sekandar Drug Centre. In his cross-examination PW 1 admitted that he did not see Dr. Rahman to sell medicine, However, he denied the defence suggestion that Bishnapada was the attendant of Dr. Golam Rahman. He further stated he could not secure the signature of accused Samir Kumar Das as he escaped from the shop. He also said that at the time of inspection of the shop there were about 50 persons present. He said no seized item was produced in the Court. PW 1 denied the defence suggestions that he filed the false case against the accused persons at the instance of Deputy Commissioner and that no medicine was seized from M/s. Rahman Clinic and the medicine seized from other shops were shown as alamats in this case. He admitted that no name of any shop was written on the bottle or packet of medicines seized and he did not enquire to know whether Samir and Bishnapada were the salesmen of the said shop as he knew from before. He also admitted that Dr. Golam Rahman was not made accused in Kotwali Police Case No. 7(6)85. 

 8. PW 2 Md. Lokman Hakim, a police constable of Mymensingh Sadar force, stated that he brought to the court (Material Ext.1) from the Malkhana and the same related to Kotwali Police Station Case No. 7(6)/85 as per chalan, Ext. 6. 

 10. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan contends first, that after seizure of the medicines PW 1 lodged First Information Report on 8.6.1985 and Kotwali PS Case No. 7(6)/85 was started but in that case the appellant No. 1 was not shown as an accused and the sub-sequent report to the Judge, Drug Court, was not competent as a revisional proceeding arising out of the Kotwali PS Case No. 7(6)/85 was pending. This contention is misconceived in that mere initiation of that case does not oust the jurisdiction of the Drug Court to take cognizance of the offence in the present case as vested under section 22 of the Ordinance inasmuch as in this case the Drug Court took cognizance of the offence on a report in writing by the Superintendent of Drug. Mr. Khan could not place any thing before me to show that the Superintendent of Drug was not authorised to write the report on which the Drug Court has taken cognizance of the offence. Thus the first contention of Mr. Khan has no sub-stance. Secondly, that no drug was seized from M/s. Rahman Clinic on 8.6.1985 by the Superintendent of Drug and the drugs which were brought from Malkhana related to another criminal case and the drugs produced before the court were not identified by any witness to show that those belonged to M/s. Rahman Clinic inasmuch as the prosecution could not show that there was any mark or label showing the name of M/s. Rahman Clinic. This contention is also untenabel as no mark or label of the shop is affixed on the bottle containing medicine or the packet rather, the name of the company manufacturing the medicines in printed on the bottle or the packet. Thirdly, in view of the FIR stating no name of appellant No. 1, the subsequent complaint lodged in the Drugs Court was after thought at the instance of the Deputy Commissioner out of enmity although Dr. Golam Rahman was neither the owner of the shop nor was its manager as stated by the prosecution. It appears from the statements made by Appellant No.1 Dr. Golam Rahman that he joined Mymensingh Medical Collage only two days before the date of occurrence and was practising merely sitting in M/s. Rahman Clinic. PW 1 in cross examination also admitted that appellant Golam Rahman was an Assistant Professor of Pathology of Mymensingh Medical College and he did not see Dr. Golam Rah-man to sell any medicine. From the evidence of PW 1 it appears that Dr. Golam Rahman filed application for renewal of drug licence, paid licence fee and filed application for withdrawal of suspension order of the drug licence. But mere signing those papers and the statement of PW 3 that appellant No. 1 was the owner of the shop do not make him the owner of the shop. The statement of PW 3 is not free from doubt and was an outcome of jealousy, as defence suggestion in that PW 3 himself had admitted that M/s. Rahman Clinic is an old shop and a bigger one than his shop and also taken into consideration of the defence case as to the emmity with the Deputy Commissioner. In this view of the matter the de-fence version of the case seems to be more probable. So far appellant Bishnapada and Samir are concerned there is no evidence on record that they were sales-men of the shop except the testimony of PW 1 and PW 3 who were highly interested witnesses in this case and it is unsafe to rely upon their testimony. The prosecution could not produce any register book showing payment of salary to appellants No. 2 and 3 by the M/s. Rahman Clinic. Moreover, no evidence is on the record that he sold medicine in contravention of sections 5 and 16 of the Ordinance. Lastly, the learned Advocate submitted that the appellants did not violate provisions of sections 5 and 16 of the Drugs (Control) Ordinance, 1982. 

 14. Section 16 provides that in order to punish an accused the medicine in question must be registered or the medicine must have been manufactured, imported, distributed or sold in contravention of provision of section 8 or the same must be adulterated or spurious. From the findings of the learned Judge of the Drug Court it seems to me that the accused persons kept in stock and exhibited the medicines in the shop "in violation of provision of section 8 of the Ordinance." Section 8 does not speak of "keeping in stock or exhibiting" the medicines in a shop. It provides that on the commencement of the Ordinance registration or licence in respect of medicines mentioned in schedules shall stand cancelled and no such medicine shall be manufactured, distributed or sold after such commencement. In this case on this analysis of the evidence on record it is not found that the accused appellants or any of them manufactured the drugs in questions or imported the same or sold to anyone. The learned Judge of the Drug Court also did not arrive at any finding as to manufacture, import or sale of the medicine. His order of conviction is based on the finding of "Keeping in stock and exhibiting the medicine in the shop."(The emphasis added). Neither section 8 nor section 16 contains such expression. Penal statute must be strictly construed and a court in order to punish an accused must not introduce any word or expression in the enactment which has not been used by the makers of the law. This order of conviction in this case on the findings as quoted above is based on the expression not used by the makers of the law. This is beyond the realm of interpretation of any provision of law by a court of law. PW 1 has also not stated that Dr. Golam Rahman, Samir Kumar and Bishnupada or any one of them sold the seized drugs. Nor the prosecution produced in court any paper to show that any of the drugs seized was unregistered or the accused violated the provision of section 8 of the Ordinance. A reference to section 8 shows that medicine specified in schedules are to be registered within the date pre-scribed' from the date of commencement of the Ordinance and are to be manufactured, imported, distributed or sold within the prescribed period from the commencement of the Ordinance and thereafter there shall be no manufacture, import, distribution or sale of any such medicines. In this case prosecution failed to produce any evidence to show that the drugs seized were manufactured, or imported or sold by the appellants. Unless the prosecution is able to prove by legal evidence that the accused violated any of the provisions of sections 8 or 16 they arc not liable to be punished under section 16 of the Ordinance. Section 8 of the Ordinance, in my opinion, also casts a duty on the prosecution to prove that the medicines also fall within any of the categories mentioned in schedules I, II, or III referred to in section 8(2). Section 5 of the Ordinance provides that no medicine shall be manufactured for sale or to be imported, distributed or sold unless it is registered with the Licensing Officer. In the instant case from the evidence it appears to me that the prosecution also failed to prove any infringement of section 5 of the Ordinance, It is also necessary to point out that the prosecution must prove that seized articles were sold. In this case there is no such evidence. In view of the evidence on record and the legal position in the case the impugned order must be struck down. Accordingly, I allow the appeal and set aside the order of conviction and sentence. I find the appellants Dr. Golam Rahman, Samir Kumar Das and Bishnupada Bhattacharjee not guilty of the charge framed against them and I acquit them from the charge. They are released from their respective bail bonds.
